For a brief moment, little more than half a minute, Tanya Plibersek articulates what is wrong with One Nation. She captures the obstruction and the hypocrisy. She circles the emptiness. Barnaby Joyce blinks slowly as he watches, swallowing like a bullfrog in a quilted vest.

“We get it,” Plibersek says. “We know that the system has not been working. Unfortunately, One Nation is not the answer to that. One Nation is the party that says workers should be paid less and easier to sack. One Nation is the party that’s voted against every cost-of-living measure that we’ve tried to introduce as a government.

“They’ve voted against cheaper electricity. They’ve voted against cheaper childcare. They’ve voted against free TAFE. And they’ve got a leader who while she’s saying workers should be easier to sack and paid less is flying around the country on Gina Rinehart’s private jet.”

This should be the Labor line, but it’s not. Like every centrist party in the world, they are still too anxious to properly repudiate their far-right challenger. They legitimise their appeal. They indulge their scant policies. In the same interview, Plibersek says: “We see those polls and we get the message.”

Rather than rejecting outright the anti-immigration rhetoric, the lies about housing and people who “look like they’ve recently arrived”, she is ready with her own numbers to prove Labor’s shared harshness: “We should be the right size Australia for our national interest, and we’ve seen immigration come down 45 per cent since we came to government…”

Anthony Albanese did exactly the same thing after Monday’s Newspoll showed One Nation outperforming Labor on primary votes: “I want an Australia that is united, one that has social cohesion at our core, one that respects people for who they are but is patriotic about all of us being Australians. We will reduce that overseas migration over the next couple of years down to 225,000 and we think that’s the right number.”

One Nation says it has raised $2 million this week. With Tony Abbott as president, the Liberal Party will do a preference swap at the next election. There is no doubting that Pauline Hanson’s party is well resourced and surging in popularity.

The answer, however, is not to join in demonising foreigners. It is not to go into interviews with a sheaf of cuts and numbers that prove migrants are the problem. It is not to link social cohesion to reducing the intake.

The answer is the one Plibersek gave to start with: the proof of what One Nation really is, a racist Potemkin controlled by billionaire donors, unconcerned with the rights of workers or with reform of any kind.

In an exclusive interview, the prime minister outlines his plans to fight One Nation, his views on Gina Rinehart and his faith in Labor as the only party that can govern in its own right.
